nameStory: The common looper moth gets its name from its caterpillar's distinctive way of moving - it arches its body into loops as it crawls, since it lacks the middle pairs of legs that most caterpillars have. This looping motion looks like someone making cursive 'l' letters across leaves and stems. The scientific name 'precationis' means 'prayer' in Latin, possibly referring to the way the larva holds its front end up while feeding.
description: The common looper moth is a medium-sized brown moth that you might spot fluttering around porch lights on warm evenings. With wings spanning about 1.5 inches across, it has mottled brown and gray coloring that helps it blend perfectly with tree bark during the day. Like many moths in the cutworm family, it holds its wings in a tent-like shape when at rest. This widespread species is one of our most reliable moth neighbors, active from spring through fall.

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Look for subtle silvery or pale markings on the brown forewings that catch the light - these often form incomplete loops or curved lines that shimmer when the moth moves

idTips.label: Size and wingspan
idTips.description: About the size of your thumb when wings are spread, roughly 1.2 to 1.5 inches across - larger than a clothes moth but smaller than a luna moth

idTips.label: Resting posture
idTips.description: Sits with wings folded in a triangular tent shape over its body, pressed flat against tree bark or house siding during daylight hours

idTips.label: Wing texture
idTips.description: Wings have a slightly fuzzy, velvety feel if you gently touch them, with scales that rub off like fine powder on your fingers

idTips.label: Flight pattern
idTips.description: Flies in an erratic, bouncing pattern around lights at night, often spiraling inward rather than flying in straight lines

habitat: You'll find common looper moths throughout New England's diverse landscapes, from suburban gardens to forest edges and meadows. They're especially common around areas with plenty of flowering plants and weedy areas, since their caterpillars feed on such a wide variety of plants including asters, clovers, and wild carrots. Look for them anywhere from sea level to mid-elevation mountains, particularly drawn to areas with outdoor lighting at night.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in April and May, when you might spot them at porch lights or resting on tree bark during warm afternoons. This is when the first generation starts laying eggs on tender new plant growth.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity time with multiple generations active - you'll see the most moths at lights during warm July and August evenings. Fresh adults continue emerging throughout the season as earlier generations reproduce.
seasonality.fall: Still active well into October, with the final generation preparing for winter. Late-season moths often seem more sluggish on cool mornings and may cluster around the last warm spots on sunny building walls.
seasonality.winter: Overwinters as pupae hidden in soil or leaf litter, completely out of sight until spring warmth triggers the next generation to emerge.

funFact: Common looper moth caterpillars are mathematical marvels - they can measure distances almost perfectly by stretching their bodies out straight like tiny green rulers, which is why they're also called 'inchworms' despite actually measuring closer to centimeters with each loop!
confusionNotes: Easily confused with other small brown moths at porch lights, but the common looper tends to be more grayish-brown rather than reddish-brown, and often has those telltale silvery markings. Memory trick: 'Looper has loops' - look for curved or circular pale markings on the forewings that remind you of its caterpillar's looping motion.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'cutworm moth,' the common looper's caterpillars don't actually cut plants at ground level like true cutworms do - they're leaf-feeders that rarely cause serious garden damage. The family name can be misleading since it groups together moths with very different larval feeding habits.
compareHints: Since this is the only Autographa species commonly found in New England, compare it with other noctuids like the cabbage looper moth, which has more distinct white markings, or various dart moths which tend to be more uniformly colored. The common looper's subtle silvery markings and medium size help distinguish it from both larger sphinx moths and tiny micro-moths that also visit lights.
